content.text: {"relation":"DIVERGENT","consensus_summary":"All four blind responses converge on the same primary identification: 'isles/islands' (Hebrew 'iyyim, coastlands) is a prophetic metonym for distant Gentile nations, the remote peoples at the ends of the earth who will hear of and receive God's salvation (Isa 42:4; 49:1; 51:5; Gen 10:5; Ps 97:1). Common alternatives: (a) in Revelation 6:14 and 16:20, islands moved/fleeing signify the shaking or removal of nations, kingdoms, or created stability under final judgment; (b) plain literal geography (coastlands, Cyprus, Malta, Patmos); (c) minority devotional readings of exile/isolation; (d) rare allegorical readings of the church as solid ground amid the sea of the world.","book_summary":"The book identifies the island as a set-apart, sanctified covenant people — a 'covenant-rock' rising out of the sea of nations (like a mountain breaking the surface), waiting for the law that sanctifies it; the 'island of the innocent' (Job 22:30) delivered to safety while the kingdoms fall (Rev 16:20 read as deliverance of the island, not its judgment).","consensus_core_identification":"Islands/isles = the distant Gentile nations and farthest coastlands of the earth, i.e., remote foreign peoples destined to hear and receive God's salvation.","book_core_identification":"Island = a sanctified, set-apart covenant people distinguished FROM the sea of nations — the elect remnant risen above the nations, awaiting the sanctifying law and preserved through judgment.","core_relation":"CONTRADICTS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The consensus treats the isles as the nations themselves (the Gentile world at large); the book treats the island as precisely what is separated out of that world — the covenant people over against the sea of nations. The book also reclassifies Rev 16:20 from an image of judgment/removal of powers (consensus alternative) into an image of the island's deliverance to safety while kingdoms fall, inverting the valence of that passage.","material_contradiction":"Consensus: island = the Gentile nations / the sea of peoples at the world's edge. Book: island = the sanctified people risen out of and distinguished from the sea of nations. The same figure cannot in the same sense denote both the mass of nations and the people set apart from the nations; the book's reading replaces the consensus referent rather than narrowing it. Its rare cousin in the consensus lists (church as solid ground amid the sea of the world) is explicitly marked 'rare' and 'later allegorical,' not the consensus core.","rationale":"Every blind response's primary meaning is 'distant Gentile nations/coastlands.' The book keeps some of the same proof-texts (Isa 42:4; 51:5 — the isles waiting for God's law) but assigns them a replaced referent: not far-off Gentiles awaiting salvation, but a set-apart covenant people awaiting sanctification, structurally opposed to the 'sea of nations' that the consensus says the isles ARE. It further contradicts the consensus's Revelation reading by making the fleeing island an object of rescue rather than of judgment. The closest consensus item is the rare allegorical 'church as island amid the sea' reading, but a rare, later-allegorical alternative does not make the book's core a refinement of the consensus core; the central identification is displaced. Hence DIVERGENT with partial reclassification of shared verses.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue REFINED rather than DIVERGENT: the book's 'sanctified people waiting for the law' could be read as the eschatological end-state of the consensus's Gentile coastlands (the nations who wait for his law become God's people), and Responses C and D both list a church-as-island-amid-the-sea alternative, so the book's core is arguably a promoted alternative rather than a replacement. Additionally, Job 22:30 ('island of the innocent') gives the book a genuine KJV textual anchor the consensus never engages, and Isa 42:4/51:5 do speak of isles waiting for God's law/trust, so the printed citations lend the book more support than a pure novelty would have. Against this, Gen 10:5 ('isles of the Gentiles') and Rev 16:20 (islands fleeing in judgment) sit awkwardly with the book's reading.","confidence":"medium"}
